prompt: What do PostgreSQL's WAL, InnoDB's redo log and SQL Server's transaction log have in common?

choices.text: They are the same file format
choices.why: Each engine has its own format; the idea is shared, not the bytes.

choices.text: Backup tools are what read them
choices.why: The server itself reads them after a crash.

choices.text: Changes land there before the data files
choices.why: Right. The idea is shared; the names differ.

choices.text: They store each table's current rows
choices.why: The rows are in the data files; the log holds changes.

prompt: Why does a new connection add a line to `ps` for PostgreSQL but not for MySQL?

choices.text: Processes versus threads
choices.why: Right. One line per process.

choices.text: MySQL hides its connections from the operating system
choices.why: Nothing is hidden: threads exist, and ps lists them when asked with -L.

choices.text: MySQL refuses connections from the same machine
choices.why: sudo mysql connected from the same machine.

choices.text: PostgreSQL forks once for each query
choices.why: Per connection, not per query.

prompt: Match each engine to the name of its page cache.
hint: One of them puts it inside a larger shared area.

prompt: A colleague says MySQL needs no change log because it has the binary log. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Nothing; the binary log is InnoDB's change log
choices.why: InnoDB has its own redo log; the binary log sits beside it.

choices.text: InnoDB keeps a redo log beside the binary log
choices.why: Right. Redo for crash repair, binlog for replication and recovery.

choices.text: The binary log was removed in MySQL 8.0
choices.why: The capture lists binlog.000001 to binlog.000003 on 8.0.

choices.text: Change logs are a PostgreSQL idea
choices.why: All four write one.

prompt: In MySQL, what does `CREATE SCHEMA billing` create?

choices.text: A database, listed by SHOW DATABASES
choices.why: Right. Schema and database are synonyms there.

choices.text: A namespace inside the current database
choices.why: That is what PostgreSQL does. MySQL has no level between server and tables.

choices.text: A user called billing
choices.why: That would be Oracle's link between schema and user.

choices.text: An error: MySQL does not have schemas
choices.why: The statement succeeds; the word is accepted.

prompt: In Oracle, what happens when you create a user called sales?

choices.text: A role waiting to be granted
choices.why: The user and its schema exist at once; privileges are separate.

choices.text: A pluggable database called sales is created
choices.why: A PDB is created separately and is a larger thing.

choices.text: An empty schema called sales comes with it
choices.why: Right. A table belongs to the user who owns it.

choices.text: A login on the instance and nothing in any database
choices.why: That is SQL Server's split, not Oracle's.

prompt: Somebody can log in to a SQL Server instance but is refused by the database shop. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: Their password expired
choices.why: Then the login would have failed.

choices.text: shop is in another schema
choices.why: A database is not inside a schema; it is the other way round.

choices.text: Their login has no user in shop
choices.why: Right. A login gets into the instance; a user gets into a database.

choices.text: The instance is in single-user mode for maintenance
choices.why: Then they could not have logged in either.

prompt: On PostgreSQL, a report needs to join a table in database shop with one in database billing. What is true?
hint: A connection is to exactly one database.

choices.text: It works if both are on the same cluster
choices.why: Same cluster or not, a plain query sees one database.

choices.text: A plain query cannot do it
choices.why: Right. Schemas join freely; databases do not.

choices.text: It works as in MySQL, with database.table
choices.why: In PostgreSQL that dotted name is schema.table.

choices.text: A superuser may run it, others may not
choices.why: Privilege is not the obstacle; the connection is.

prompt: Match each engine to what its outermost box is called.
Why did `sudo mysql` connect with no password on Ubuntu?
hint: Same idea as sudo -u postgres psql.

choices.text: root has no password in a fresh MySQL
choices.why: There is no password to be empty: auth_socket never asks for one.

choices.text: sudo passes the password along by itself
choices.why: sudo knows nothing about MySQL passwords.

choices.text: The kernel tells MySQL who is on the socket
choices.why: Right. The peer check under another name.

choices.text: MySQL trusts local connections
choices.why: Only root@localhost uses auth_socket; the other accounts use passwords.

prompt: In /var/lib/mysql, which entry plays the part pg_wal plays for PostgreSQL?

choices.text: ibdata1
choices.why: InnoDB's shared space, not its log.

choices.text: binlog.000001
choices.why: The binary log, a second log for replication.

choices.text: mysql.ibd
choices.why: That holds MySQL's own system tables.

choices.text: #innodb_redo
choices.why: Right. The redo log is the change log.

prompt: MySQL lists root with host localhost. What does the host column change?

choices.text: Nothing; it is a comment
choices.why: It is part of the account's identity.

choices.text: It limits root to the binary log
choices.why: Host has nothing to do with logs.

choices.text: It decides which database is the default
choices.why: The default database is chosen on connection, not by host.

choices.text: It is part of the account
choices.why: Right. user@host is the account.

prompt: After `CREATE SCHEMA billing` in the PostgreSQL database ana, why does `\l` not list billing?

choices.text: The schema was created in another cluster
choices.why: It went into the database the session was connected to.

choices.text: It sits one level lower
choices.why: Right. \dn shows it.

choices.text: The schema needs a commit to appear
choices.why: psql commits each statement by itself.

choices.text: Schemas are hidden from \l for safety
choices.why: \dn showed it to ana, and would to anyone.

prompt: On Ubuntu, MySQL's error log is the file ___ in /var/log/mysql.
Why does Oracle have no autovacuum?

choices.text: Its tables are append-only
choices.why: Oracle tables change like any other.

choices.text: RMAN removes dead rows during backups
choices.why: RMAN backs up; it does not clean tables.

choices.text: Old row versions go to undo, not the table
choices.why: Right. Nothing is left in the table for a vacuum to remove.

choices.text: It runs VACUUM FULL at night
choices.why: There is no such command in Oracle.

prompt: SQL Server's recovery model FULL keeps the transaction log for point-in-time restore. What decides the same thing on PostgreSQL?
hint: Keeping the log after the server is done with it.

choices.text: Archiving the WAL
choices.why: Right. db-reliability's lessons 4 and 6.

choices.text: Running ANALYZE more often
choices.why: ANALYZE gathers statistics; it keeps no log.

choices.text: Setting fsync = off
choices.why: That risks the data; it keeps nothing.

choices.text: Creating a tablespace for the log
choices.why: Where the log lives does not decide whether it is kept.

prompt: Match each term to its nearest PostgreSQL counterpart.
What does PostgreSQL answer to `SELECT '1abc' = 1`?

choices.text: An error
choices.why: Right. It will not guess.

choices.text: true, with a warning
choices.why: That is MySQL's answer.

choices.text: false
choices.why: It does not compare at all; the conversion fails first.

choices.text: NULL
choices.why: NULL would mean unknown; here it refuses.

prompt: Which reason given for using PostgreSQL in this course is specific to learning administration?
hint: Settings, statistics and logs in front of you.

choices.text: It is the fastest of the four engines
choices.why: The course makes no such claim.

choices.text: It shows its working
choices.why: Right. A file you can read, a view you can query.

choices.text: It needs less configuration
choices.why: Lesson 5 is about its configuration.

choices.text: Oracle and SQL Server are being retired
choices.why: Both are sold and widely used.

prompt: A manager asks for "a new database for the invoicing service" on a MySQL server. What do you create?
hint: Which level does the word mean there?

choices.text: A second mysqld on another port
choices.why: That is a second server, much more than was asked.

choices.text: One more entry in SHOW DATABASES
choices.why: Right. On MySQL the word means that level.

choices.text: A user called invoicing that owns its tables
choices.why: That is the Oracle reading.

choices.text: A tablespace called invoicing
choices.why: A tablespace is about where files live, not a namespace.

prompt: A server runs out of disk because its change log keeps growing. Which lesson's ideas carry over if the engine is SQL Server?

choices.text: Lesson 12, on GRANT
choices.why: Privileges do not fill a disk.

choices.text: Lesson 18, on extensions
choices.why: Extensions are not involved.

choices.text: Lesson 7, on the write-ahead log
choices.why: Right. Same mechanism, another name.

choices.text: Lesson 22, on schema changes
choices.why: It is SQL Server's change log.

prompt: Order PostgreSQL's levels from the outermost to the innermost.
trap: Schema before database is MySQL's mix-up carried over: in PostgreSQL schemas live inside a database.
